rows.name: Data Workers' Inquiry
aka: Workers' Inquiry as a Research Methodology (WIRM)
rows.operator: Distributed AI Research Institute (DAIR) and the Weizenbaum Institute, with TU Berlin; project lead Milagros Miceli
rows.kind: global, radically participatory research initiative; community-based research project with a public repository of worker-made inquiries
rows.unit: an inquiry: one data worker's research in their own workplace, published in a format the worker chose (zine, documentary, comic, essay, podcast, animation, report)
rows.labor_object: data labeling, content moderation, data annotation, chatbot impersonation and other data processing that enables AI systems, done by workers at outsourcing companies and platforms (Sama, Cloud Factory, Remotasks, Telus International, Scale AI, Amazon Mechanical Turk, TikTok and Apple's outsourced workforce among those named); invited pieces extend it to artists, translators, writers, nurses and internet users who produce data for AI without compensation

direction.supplies: data workers, often in the Global Majority, precariously employed and politically dispersed, as the project states; in the inquiries, content moderators and annotators in Kenya, Syria, Lebanon, Venezuela, Brazil, Germany, France, Spain and the UK
direction.directs: outsourcing companies and platforms, as the inquiries name them (Sama, Cloud Factory, Remotasks, Telus International, Scale AI, Amazon Mechanical Turk), working for client firms named in the inquiries (Meta, TikTok, Apple)
direction.gains: not recorded as a quantity; the inquiries record the costs workers bear (psychological trauma, low pay, unpaid time, gift-card payment, account shutdowns, layoffs) and name the firms the work serves

rows.method: worker-written inquiry: participatory action research in which data workers act as community researchers, set their own questions, design and conduct the inquiry (interviews with colleagues among them) and choose the presentation format; the organizing team trains them in data collection and analysis and monitors legal and ethical boundaries

coverage.geography: nine countries across five continents (the home page); Kenya, Venezuela, Syria, Lebanon and Germany at launch
coverage.period: project phase at the Weizenbaum Institute August 2023 to November 2024; the repository continues on data-workers.org (copyright 2026)

unit.quote: Each GDPval task consists of two primary components: a request (often with reference files) and a deliverable (work product).

task_origin.quote: Each task is constructed based on actual work product created by an expert professional.

supplies.quote: Tasks are constructed from the representative work of industry professionals with an average of 14 years of experience.

recruitment.quote: Experts were required to have a minimum of 4 years of professional experience in their occupation and a strong resume with a demonstrated history of professional recognition, promotion, and management responsibilities. The average expert had 14 years of experience. We further required experts to pass a video interview, a background check, a training and a quiz to participate in the project. Experts were well compensated for their time and experience.

recruitment_selectivity.quote: Less than 10% of applicants were selected to contribute tasks to our full set.

vendors.quote: We are also grateful to our vendor partners for their collaboration and support throughout this research, and extend a special thank you to the industry experts who contributed their time and expertise to GDPval

review.quote: All 1,320 tasks in the full GDPval set went through an iterative review pipeline involving both automated model-based screening and multiple stages of human expert review. Each task received an average of five human reviews (with a minimum of three reviews).

directs_research_team.quote: Initially, our researchers manually reviewed all tasks to identify experts who produced consistently high-quality tasks; these individuals were trained and promoted to reviewers.

directs_models.quote: Experts retained final responsibility for task accuracy and completeness; the model did not autonomously alter tasks.

grading.quote: we conducted blinded expert pairwise comparisons, where experts in the relevant occupation were presented with a request and reference files and asked to rank two or more unlabeled work deliverables.

grading_time.quote: On average, grading each comparison for the gold subset took over an hour.

automated_grader.quote: achieves 66% agreement with human expert graders, only 5% below human expert inter-rating agreement of 71%.

task_value.quote: Each task’s dollar value was estimated by multiplying the average estimated completion time by median hourly wages for the corresponding occupation from OEWS data

task_length.quote: Tasks require an average of 7 hours of work for an expert professional to complete. On the high end, tasks span up to multiple weeks of work.

finding_trend.quote: Figure 6: Performance of OpenAI frontier models increased roughly linearly over time on the GDPval gold subset.

finding_parity.quote: Figure 5: On human pairwise comparisons, models are beginning to approach parity with industry experts on the GDPval gold subset.

finding_claude.quote: on the GDPval gold subset, 47.6% of deliverables by Claude Opus 4.1 were graded as better than (wins) or as good as (ties) the human deliverable. Model deliverables outperformed or matched expert humans’ deliverables in just over half the tasks.

finding_strengths.quote: Claude Opus 4.1 was the best performing model on the GDPval gold subset, excelling in particular on aesthetics (e.g., document formatting, slide layout), while GPT-5 excelled in particular on accuracy (e.g., carefully following instructions, performing correct calculations)

finding_instructions.quote: Figure 8: Across models, experts most often preferred the human deliverable because models failed to fully follow instructions on GDPval tasks.

finding_review_redo.quote: When incorporating time to review and redo work, the payoff from using a model shrinks.

fix_it_setup.quote: Here, an expert human samples from a model, reviews outputs, and if unsatisfactory, resamples and repeats. If no satisfactory output is obtained, the human completes the task themselves.

finding_failures.quote: Another roughly 29% of ratings were for bad or catastrophic (with roughly 3% of failures marked as catastrophic).

finding_length.quote: Win rates are highest for shorter tasks (0–2 hours) and decline steadily as completion time increases.

finding_scaffolding.quote: We also demonstrate that increased reasoning effort, increased task context, and increased scaffolding improves model performance on GDPval.

gains_wage_basis.quote: Because our experts were recruited specifically for being highly experienced in their field, these wage estimates likely underestimate their true market cost.

limit_size.quote: The GDPval full set currently consists of only 44 occupations and 30 total tasks per occupation. It is therefore a limited, initial cut of knowledge work tasks, not a comprehensive evaluation of all possible occupational tasks. We are expanding the dataset size.

limit_scope.quote: Manual labor and physical tasks are not included in the current version. limit_one_shot.quote: For GDPval, we provide the full context of the task in the prompt, but in real life it often takes effort to figure out the full context of a task and understand what to work on.

limit_cost.quote: Constructing and running our evaluation is expensive, particularly with industry expert graders. For this reason, we make an automated grader proxy available, but do not consider it a full substitute for industry expert graders.

limit_grader_self.quote: Our automated grader, based on GPT-5-high, shows lower correlation with human expert graders when assessing outputs from capable OpenAI models. This aligns with empirical evidence that models often favor their own responses

limit_savings.quote: We do not include consideration of the time taken to review a human professional deliverable, although this would commonly occur for tasks in GDPval (either self-review of the professional’s own work or review by a supervisor of a team member’s work). One further limitation of this analysis is that it does not capture the cost of catastrophic mistakes, which can be disproportionately expensive in some domains.

limit_self_report.quote: Because times were self-reported, it is possible that experts under-estimated or over-estimated time taken

limit_blinding.quote: We aimed to keep comparisons as blind as possible, but model samples may still have been identifiable due to stylistic differences.

limit_under_context.quote: As a note: this experiment was run on an earlier version of the GDPval gold subset, and therefore the observed win rates do not match those in the main text of the paper.

data_access_ungradable.quote: In the open-source set we mark 12 out of 220 tasks as ungradable due to limitations of the automated grader.

lifecycle.quote: Future GDPval iterations will incorporate greater breadth, realism, interactivity, and contextual nuance.

self_description.quote: In collaboration with ADP Research, we summarize live labor market trends for a sample workers in firms using ADP payroll services.

method.quote: Using a sample of high-frequency administrative payroll data from ADP covering millions of U.S. workers through June 2026, we document six facts about the labor market following the widespread adoption of generative AI.

method_sample.quote: We adopt the balanced sample approach of Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen (2025) , including firms with 5 years of employment history in ADP.

method_rolling.quote: Each month, we roll this 5-year window forward. We additionally limit our sample to workers successfully matched to an occupation code.

uses_aei.quote: We match the occupation-level ADP data to various measures of exposure: Eloundou et al. (2024) and the Anthropic Economic Index .

count.quote: As of the Canaries Dashboard launch, our balanced sample of firms using ADP payroll services, spanning the 5 years ending in April 2026, consists of 25,000 firms. In November 2022, these firms employed 4.6mm workers successfully matched to an occupation code. This sample covers over 730 unique occupations.

finding_no_displacement.quote: We find no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement.

finding_19.quote: However, employment of young workers (ages 22–25) in AI-exposed occupations now stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with that of their less-exposed peers; experienced workers show no comparable gap.

founded.quote: This divergence has widened steadily since we first documented it in August 2025.

finding_hiring.quote: It operates primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations.

finding_substitution.quote: Declines are concentrated in occupations where AI usage primarily substitutes for human tasks; where usage primarily complements workers, employment is flat or rising, especially for experienced workers

finding_compensation.quote: Adjustment is occurring through employment rather than base compensation.

finding_automation_ratio.quote: However, the automation ratio shows a clear correlation with employment trends: occupations with a higher share of automation in total usage see declines or more muted increases in the employment index.

finding_gender.quote: In the most-exposed quintile, employment among early-career women has been contracting at 4.5% per year since the introduction of ChatGPT in November 2022, while employment for men of the same age is contracting at 2.5% per year.

finding_gender_2.quote: Accordingly, gender-based differences in the relationship between AI exposure and employment trends appear to be driven primarily by occupational composition, rather than disparate trends within given sets of occupations.

limit_causal.quote: We interpret these facts as early, descriptive indicators—canaries in the coal mine—rather than causal estimates

limit_attenuate.quote: These patterns attenuate when controlling for education, show some divergent trends predating generative AI, and are more pronounced in the ADP analysis sample than in national survey benchmarks, with some evidence of consistent patterns in government administrative data.

limit_sample.quote: Our sample represents neither the entire U.S. labor market nor the universe of firms using ADP payroll services.

limit_entry_exit.quote: This restriction shuts down the margins of firm entry and exit.

limit_correlation.quote: Accordingly, the Canaries Dashboard measures the correlation between occupational exposure measures and employment trends in our sample, rather than a causal link between the two.

limit_2024.quote: when including the broadest set of controls, declines in AI-exposed occupations become statistically significant in 2024. The earlier declines are likely driven by non-AI factors.

self_description.quote: This study updates the ILO’s 2023 Global Index of Occupational Exposure to Generative AI (GenAI), incorporating recent advances in the technology and increasing user familiarity with GenAI tools.

method.quote: Using a representative sample from the 29,753 tasks in the Polish occupational classification system and a survey of 1,640 people employed in each 1-digit ISCO-08 groups, we collect 52,558 data points regarding perceive potential of automation for 2,861 tasks.

method_2.quote: We then compare this input with a survey and several rounds of Delphi-style discussions among a smaller group of international experts.

method_llm.quote: relying on three advanced LLMs available on the market at the end of 2024: GPT-4, GPT-4o and Gemini Flash 1.5.

method_predictor.quote: Using this approach, we generate predictions for all 29,753 tasks in the Polish classification system (Table 1).

method_isco.quote: we use the same system to predict automation scores for 3,265 tasks in ISCO-08

survey_design.quote: This means that tasks of managers are assessed by individuals working as managers, tasks of professionals are assessed by professionals, etc.

occupations.quote: At the most detailed, 6-digit level, this framework contains 2541 occupations and 29,753 corresponding tasks (Table 1).

unit.quote: we rely on two moments of distribution: occupational mean and standard deviation (SD) of task-level scores pertaining to a given 4-digit occupation.

exposed_occupations.quote: we focus on the 112 occupations identified as exposed and estimate the share of employment that these occupations represent at the global, regional, and income-based levels.

employment_model.quote: This model is based on a harmonized microdata collection and a hierarchical imputation process

finding_global.quote: Globally, one in four workers are in an occupation with some GenAI exposure. 3.3% of global employment falls into the highest exposure category, albeit with significant differences between female (4.7%) and male employment (2.4%).

finding_income.quote: These differences increase with countries’ income (9.6% female vs 3.5% male in Gradient 4 in HICs), and so does the overall exposure (11% of total employment in LICs vs 34% in HICs).

finding_24.quote: one in four jobs globally (24%) has some degree of exposure, and one in three jobs in high-income countries.

finding_clerical.quote: Clerical occupations continue to have the highest exposure levels. Additionally, some strongly digitized occupations have increased exposure

finding_scores.quote: Overall, the automation scores are slightly lower than in 2023 (a mean automation score of 0.29 in 2025 versus 0.30 in 2023), though the variability of scores is considerably lower (standard deviation 0.14 in 2025 v. 0.30 in 2023).

finding_transformed.quote: One in four workers across the world are in an occupation with some degree of GenAI exposure, but because of the continued need for human input, most jobs will be transformed rather than made redundant.

gains.quote: the key to unlocking the productivity benefits of GenAI lies not in the search of outright labour savings, but in the extent to which human expertise can be complemented with new technological capacities to reshape occupations and generate additional value-added

limit.quote: It is important to stress that these new estimates reflect “exposure” to GenAI and not the actual impact on employment. As in 2023, the 2025 estimates represent the upper threshold of the percentage of employment that could be affected if GenAI technology were fully implemented.

limit_2.quote: Finally, the estimates do not account for new jobs that may be created, nor the technological advances that could potentially automate more tasks in the future. In that sense, our estimates present a static snapshot of the exposure of existing occupations to GenAI at the start of 2025.

limit_3.quote: On the downside, this survey design means that the sample may not represent the entire working population, and interpretability of opinions on the automation potential is limited to comparisons within each 1-digit group.

limit_4.quote: For 91.5% of the tasks, respondents did not report performing a similar task in their work

limit_5.quote: The new global index presented in this paper is generic, due to the nature of ISCO-08 and the structure of tasks associated with occupations in this framework.

limit_6.quote: we stress that such exposure does not imply the immediate automation of an entire occupation, but rather the potential for a large share of its current tasks to be performed using this technology.
